title: Final Reflection
text:
Reflection should include:
* how each one ties into class content
All of the mini-projects that we had in this course tie directly into the specific sections that they were designed to follow. After each completion of a section, the mini-project helped solidify theoretical ideas which related to the main themes of the course. There are aspects though where we see the mini-projects connecting to other sections too, and looking back at all the coursework we can see how certain projects had us prepare for certain sections or return to ideas from previous sections. Beginning with mini-project 1, which heavily connected to the first section of notes on sampling distributions. In this project we simulated distributions for the minimum and maximum of various probability distributions. This connected both the ideas we saw in the first note packet, sampling distributions and order statistics. In the labs for the first section, we used statistical simulation to look at how sampling distributions could change. This mini-project was directly similar to this concept, just a bit more complex as we used more than one type of probability distribution. We can also see connections in all of the later sections, as we continuously saw the concept of a sampling distribution reappear, and we also continued to utilize statistical simulation in most of the labs and other mini-projects within the course.
We then worked through Mini-project 2, which seemed to connect to all of the sections in the course, but less so to the section devoted to Bayesian statistics. This mini-project solidified our understanding of extremely important vocabulary, thus creating a foundation we could expand upon in later sections. A majority of these words had been introduced to us in our section on estimation (bias, consistent, variance, etc.) but there was also some which we had learned in section 1. As we worked through the class we continued to see a lot of these words (such as likelihood, parameter). Naturally, this mini-project connected to section 2 on estimation, where we derived a lot of estimators and estimates for different distributions and focused on their variance and bias. This project differed from the others because it didn’t have any similar computations to the section that it followed, it was strictly completed to increase our knowledge of the vocabulary. Mini-project 3 connected to the section based on confidence intervals, but it also had some overlap with section 5 on hypothesis testing. In this mini-project, we saw ways that the intervals would vary when given different parameters (proportion and sample size). This expanded on the notes and examples we worked through in section 3, where we learned how to calculate and interpret confidence intervals based on data, but the mini-project helped incorporate statistical simulation and understand how confidence intervals would react to unmet assumptions. This idea of breaking or meeting assumptions tied into the section on hypothesis testing, as we saw assumptions as being very important for test statistics which rely on the Central Limit Theorem.
Mini-project 4 was unique, as it really only connected to the section 4 coursework. This section was different because it focused specifically on Bayesian statistics, and not frequentist statistics like all of the other sections. During this section, we focused on deriving posterior distributions from various prior distributions. These prior distributions were either non-informative or were created using a priori knowledge. Mini-project 4 directly relates to this idea as we used various informative and non-informative priors to display how they can alter the posterior distribution. Another way that this connected was through the creation of informative priors, which we could make based on knowledge from ‘experts’ and this was done in both our section coursework and the mini-project. Our last mini-project was also quite unique, like the mini-project from section 2 it didn’t have to do with computations. This mini-project was basically an analysis of the paper ‘Moving to a world beyond p<0.05’ by Wasserstein, Schirm, and Lazar. In this project we focused on understanding why using p-values and confidence intervals may not be the best practice, and how these values are seen as extremely reliable when in reality they are made based on data, not the truth. In the notes for section 5, we spend a lot of time learning how to calculate and interpret p-values, so this paper added a layer to our understanding of how we should be drawing conclusions and looking at results. Although this project didn’t directly connect to the computations in the course, I thought it was a nice closing project and an enriching paper that helped us not just understand the metrics we have learned about, but the ways they are used in research.
* how they connect to eachother
Not only do these projects connect to the course material, but we can see ways in which the min-projects connect to eachother.
mini-project 1 mini-project 2 mini-project 3 mini-project 4 mini-project 5
* biggest takeaways from the projects
Each of these mini-projects had valuable lessons which applied to our coursework, but there were specific things that I took away from them. From the first mini-project, I learned more about the differences between some of the probability distributions we had focused on in STAT 325. Looking at the expected value and variances of the min/max showed me how the spread of each of these distributions can differ, and this project also really showed me how impactful statistical simulation is. The biggest takeaway that I took from the second mini-project is a little less theoretical. By writing this meaningful story I was able to work all of the vocab words together, and this helped strengthen my understanding of what they really mean (aside from a strict definition). The biggest takeaway that I took from the third mini-project relates to how broken assumptions will affect confidence intervals. When these assumptions are broken it can alter the width and coverage rate of the interval, which then affects the accuracy of your confidence interval interpretation. Through the fourth mini-project, I learned how influential the prior distribution is to the posterior distribution, and that by using different prior distributions you can create entirely different posterior distributions (which will then affect your conclusions). The idea I really took from this is the benefit to being able to adjust your distributions based on pre-existing knowledge (or with the addition of more data), which is unique to Bayesian stats. Lastly, the takeaway that I had from the fifth mini-project is that the reliance we have on p-values and confidence intervals is misguided and actually is limiting the scope of scientific research. From this paper, I learned the dangers of the strict division that significance contributes to research studies, and I also learned some opinions on how we should try to change this and approach results in a different way.

title: Simulation to Investigate Confidence Intervals
text:
Code for simulations!
For my simulations I reran the code below and just changed the n and p values

library(tidyverse)
qnorm(0.95)

[1] 1.644854

make_prop_df<- function(n,p){
  
  x <- rbinom(1, n, p) # randomly generate number of successes for the sample
  ## number of successes divided by sample size
  phat <- x / n
  lb <- phat - 1.64*sqrt(phat*(1-phat)/n)
  ub <- phat + 1.64*sqrt(phat*(1-phat)/n)
  
  prop_df<-tibble(phat,lb,ub)
  return(prop_df)
}

nsim<-5000
prop_ci_df<-map(1:nsim,
    \(i) make_prop_df(n=largeN, p=p2))|>
  bind_rows()


prop_ci_df|> mutate(width = ub - lb, 
                    in_cover = ifelse(lb <= p2 & p2 <= ub, 1,0))|>
  summarise(avg_width = mean(width),
            coverage = mean(in_cover))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  avg_width coverage
      <dbl>    <dbl>
1    0.0586    0.897

Summary of my findings
In my table of results the first thing that I am drawn to is the difference in average width across the settings. I can see that as n increases the width of my confidence intervals narrow, with the average width getting smaller. This makes sense, as we increase the amount of observations we have we can get a better understanding of where the value will truly lie, allowing us to decrease the width of our interval. I can also see that the average widths are a bit wider at my higher p value than at the lower value. This change is not very large but potentially something to note. We can really see this pattern at n = 5, where the width differs between the two “p” values by about 0.17. It is not as clear to me why this would be the case, but perhaps because the value varies from 0.5 and has such a small n, something happens to the precision of the CIs.
Looking at the coverage rates, I can see that at the n=500 settings the coverage rates were around 90%, as expected! At n = 30, the rates are lower but very similar, falling at 86.2% and 85.5%. This is interesting to me because I would have assumed that the setting n = 30 and p = 0.6 would have a rate close to 90%, since it met the “large sample” assumption. Lastly, the n=5 coverage rates, which differ greatly based on the proportion they were given. For the higher p value close to 0.5, the n=5 did not do a horrible job with a rate of 82.5%, however this is much lower than we would expect for a 90% confidence interval. For the p=0.2 and n=5 condition we can see that this simulations confidence intervals did not do well at all, with a coverage rate of 61.4%.
Looking at these results I can make some conclusions about the ways that parameters may influence confidence intervals. As mentioned above I can see that as you increase n, the confidence intervals will become more narrow. Based on the n=5 settings I can also see by looking at both coverage rate and average interval width that failing both of the assumptions will lead to a poor coverage rate and a wide interval (especially when the proportion value differs from 0.5). Another conclusion I would suggest is that a “p” value which differs from 0.5 greatly will result in narrower intervals, which can be seen in the last row of my results table. Lastly, another conclusion I would suggest is that if the n value is large enough, the lower “p” value will not be able to affect the intervals as strongly. I make this assumption because i can see that the n=30 and p=0.2 condition preformed similarly to the n=30 & p=0.6 condition, even though the former failed the “large sample” assumption.

title: A Meaningful Story
text:
Mini-Project Goal:
Portray your understanding of relevant vocabulary words by writing them into an understandable story.


Story
Landing on the planet Gorbly was a rocky ride, the shuttle landed abruptly, shocking 10 of Earth’s most awarded scientists and statisticians who had descended here to determine the suitability of this new planet. Their goal was to secure a food resource before the remaining 500 humans arrived from Earth. Luckily through prior research they believed they had found the answer to their problem, a large watermelon-like fruit which contained every possible vitamin a human would need. What luck! Through initial surveillance they believed that the size and weight of the fruit followed a normal distribution, however they needed a strategy to estimate a parameter, since the true mean of the fruit’s weight remained unclear. They quickly began their assessment and chose a random sample of 10 groves which contained 30 fruits each. They decided that this was an appropriate number of random variables because each scientist could harvest and weigh the fruits in their own grove. Like the general population of these fruits they assumed that each of these variables followed a normal distribution. Now that they had all this data the scientists were lost, wondering how they could use this to come up with an estimate. Thank goodness for Kaitlin Heintzman, Earth’s top statistician who recalled that they could create an estimator that maximized the likelihood; by then inputting their sample they could find a more accurate estimate than something with less likelihood! Kaitlin had brought along her undergrad notes from math stat, and using this she identified a maximum likelihood estimator for the mean of this alien cuisine. The estimation for the mean ended up being just the mean of the data, which using the data they collected from their random sample created an estimate of 10 pounds. Another statistician on the trip scoffed, Willy Pomfrit was a known pessimist, and he believed he had a better estimator! He said that the estimator for the unknown parameter should be based on the expectation and variance of the lightest grove (the minimum). Using his estimators he calculated that the mean estimate was 5 pounds*. Now they had a dilemma, which estimator was better?? Assessing the estimated mean, the bias of Kaitlin’s estimator was 0 as it was always the mean, which was better than Willy’s estimator which had a bias of 4*. The next step was to assess the variance, although Kaitlin’s may be closer to the mean than Willy’s how did the spreads compare? After this computation it was found that Kaitlin’s estimator had a variance of 2, and Willy’s was a variance of 3*. With these computations complete the group of scientists were convinced that Kaitlin’s was the better estimator of the two and they were almost convinced that they should choose hers. The crew only had 30 minutes before the second ship was supposed to enter Gorbly’s atmosphere and they needed to solidify their estimate!! The last test that would convince the crew was to check the consistency of the estimator. If they figured how to grow these fruits to an infinitely large population, would the expected value approach the true mean, and would the variance approach zero?? Kaitlin was confident in her estimator, but nervous as the minutes ticked down. Finally, the calculations were done, and they found the estimator WAS consistent! The crew was able to place confidence in this estimator and estimate and would be able to ensure that the rest of humanity would have an adequate food source on the planet Gorbly.
*Note that the bias and variance for Willy’s estimator are completely made up for the plot of the story.

title: Bayesian Analysis
text:
Explore a Bayesian approach to data analysis. Understand how different priors affect posterior distributions.

library(tidyverse)

title: Bayesian Analysis
text:
Introduction
The goal of this project is to try to answer the question “what is the probability that Rafael Nadal wins a point on his own serve when playing against Novak Djokovic at the French Open?” by using Bayesian analysis to estimate this unknown parameter and its distribution. In this project, I will use various priors combined with data from the 2020 French Open to construct three posterior distributions, I will analyze the differences that I find along the way and how each distributions predicts the probability of interest.

title: Bayesian Analysis
text:
Priors
prior_1 ~ beta(1,1)
prior_2

alphas <- seq(0.001, 100, length.out = 1000)
betas <- ((1-(46/66))/(46/66)) * alphas

param_df <- tibble(alphas, betas)
param_df <- param_df |> mutate(vars = 
                    (alphas*betas)/((alphas+betas)^2*(alphas+betas+1)))


target_var <- 0.05657^2

param_df <- param_df |> mutate(dist_to_target = abs(vars - target_var))
param_df |> filter(dist_to_target == min(dist_to_target))

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  alphas betas    vars dist_to_target
   <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>          <dbl>
1   45.3  19.7 0.00320     0.00000310


For this informative prior I made the assumption that the clay-court match played in the previous year was preformed in comparable conditions to the match that I am interested in. Examples of conditions that I assume to be the same are weather (it is not considerably more sunny) and player ability (both players are not coming off of an injury or illness).
prior_3

alpha <- seq(0.001, 300, length.out = 1000)
beta<- (0.25/0.75)*alpha

tibble(alpha,beta)|>
  mutate(prob = pbeta(0.7,alpha, beta),
         dist = abs(prob - 0.02))|>
  filter(dist == min(dist))

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  alpha  beta   prob      dist
  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1  252.  83.9 0.0200 0.0000289


For this informative prior I make the assumption that the sports announcer is not bias towards one of the players, and that the announcer is also accurate at estimating performance percentages.
In my code above, I also implement my own understand of “almost sure” by denoting the distance column with a value of 0.02, whereas another person could potentially believe that this value should be larger or smaller.

  geom_line(data = plot_3, aes(x = grid, y = post_3), col = "red")+

Posterior means and 90% credible intervals
Posterior_1

57/(57+30)

[1] 0.6551724

qbeta(c(0.05, 0.95), 57, 30)

[1] 0.5697738 0.7364913


posterior mean = 0.655
credible interval = (0.5698 - 0.7365)
Posterior_2

101.3/(101.3+48.7)

[1] 0.6753333

qbeta(c(0.05, 0.95), 101.3, 48.7)

[1] 0.6113201 0.7366795


posterior mean = 0.675
credible interval = (0.6113 - 0.7367)
Posterior_3

309/(309 + 112.9)

[1] 0.732401

qbeta(c(0.05, 0.95), 309, 112.9)

[1] 0.696369 0.767179


posterior mean = 0.732
credible interval = (0.6964 - 0.7672)


Why do the posteriors look different?
The posteriors look different from each other because although they use the same data, they all came from different priors which means that their posterior distributions are directly connected to differing prior alphas and betas. This causes the staggering of means, and the difference in variance we can see in the wideness/narrowness of the distributions in the posterior plot.


Which would I choose?
I would choose the 2nd posterior distribution which used the informative prior based on the previous years match results. I would choose this posterior distribution because I believe that utilizing the previous years data would be a good base of information for our question of interest, and it has a mean which is around the middle of the other two distributions. I also believe that since we know how notable Nadal is, it is not entirely fair to use an uninformative prior. Lastly, the low variance that can be seen in the last distribution makes me not believe this would be a beneficial posterior distribution because it does not hold a lot of room for error, and it relies heavily on the information that was provided in the prior.


Why does one posterior have a lower variance?
The last posterior distribution which was created using the sports announcers previous knowledge has the lowest variance, which can be seen by the extremely narrow peak in the plot. The reason that this has such a low variance is because if both alpha and beta parameters in a gamma distribution are large the variance will be small and in this posterior distribution the posterior alpha and beta are extremely large values (due to the large parameters from the prior distribution). ## Conclusion
In this mini project, I found that the prior distribution will greatly influence your posterior distribution and therefore the conclusions that you can make about your parameter/question of interest. I can see that for binomial data, starting with large parameters in your prior will to a posterior model with low variance and a much more narrow credible interval, which seems unlikely to be helpful in situations where you may not know feel as confident in a topic (or in the information you have been given to create the prior). I also can conclude why using a non-informative prior would be beneficial in a case where you don’t have a lot of prior experience/information because it returns a posterior model with more variance, and therefore returns a wider credible interval. This would be helpful as a model to get an impression about what a proportion might be, and to then be able to potentially incorporate more data into this, which would lead to a stronger model. Above I explained that I believe the “middle” distribution (2nd prior) would be my distribution of choice and from this project I can see how using an informative prior, when the data is concrete and not speculated, potentially will lead to a good model which is not too biased towards the prior, and will return a solid credible interval and estimate for the proportion of interest.
Lastly, I can make a conclusion about our question of interest using the model that I would use! To do so I will interpret the credible interval. According to the model, there is a 90% probability that the proportion of points Rafael Nadal will win when he is serving against Noval Djokovic at the French Open is between 0.611 and 0.737.

title: Sampling Distribution of Min and Max
text:
Distribution Simulations

Normal(10,4)
To save space I will only include one chunk of code showing how I created the simulation. For the other distributions the only difference is the alteration of “rnorm” and its arguments to the function corresponding to the correct distribution. (E.g rexp(n, lambda))

n<- 5 
mu<- 10 
sigma<-2

generate_samp_min <- function(mu, sigma, n) {
  
  single_sample <- rnorm(n, mu, sigma)
  sample_min <- min(single_sample)
  
  return(sample_min)
}

generate_samp_max <- function(mu, sigma, n) {
  
  single_sample <- rnorm(n, mu, sigma)
  sample_max <- max(single_sample)
  
  return(sample_max)
}

nsim <- 5000      # number of simulations

## code to map through the function. 
## the \(i) syntax says to just repeat the generate_samp_mean function
## nsim times
mins_norm <- map_dbl(1:nsim, \(i) generate_samp_min(mu = mu, sigma = sigma, n = n))

title: Sampling Distribution of Min and Max
text:
Questions

1. Compare the SE from the sampling distribution of the maximum and the minimum for these distributions
For both the normal and uniform distributions, the standard errors are quite similar, with the uniform having a slightly higher SE for the sampling distribution of the minimum compared to the maximum. The last two (Exponential and Beta) have Standard Errors that differ greatly between the two sampling distributions. Looking at exponential, there is a clearly higher SE produced from the sampling distribution of the maximum compared to the minimum. Similarly the difference between the SEs of the sampling distributions corresponsing to the beta distribution is high (with respect to the smallness of the SEs) with a higher SE(\(y_{min}\)).These results suggest that perhaps when a distribution is symmetric (like the normal and uniform), the Standard Errors for the sampling distributions of the sample minimum and maximum will be close to equivalent. From these results I don’t believe that any conclusion or rule can be made on an non-symmetric distribution, like the beta and exponential.

title: Advantages and Drawbacks of using P-values
text: Read ‘Moving to a world beyond p<0.05’ by Wasserstein, Schirm, and Lazar. Answer questions about the reading, dissecting the disadvantages to utilizing p-values and confidence intervals in statistical results.

title: Advantages and Drawbacks of using P-values
text:
Statement of Integrity
“All work presented is my own, and I have followed all rules for collaboration. I have not used generative AI on this project.” - Kaitlin Heintzman

title: Advantages and Drawbacks of using P-values
section: Towards the end of Section 1, the authors say “As ‘statistical significance’ is used less, statistical thinking will be used more.” Elaborate on what you think the authors mean. Give some examples of what you think embodies “statistical thinking.”
text:
Towards the end of Section 1, the authors say “As ‘statistical significance’ is used less, statistical thinking will be used more.” Elaborate on what you think the authors mean. Give some examples of what you think embodies “statistical thinking.”
This refers to the idea that statistical significance is reliant upon arbitrarily set values that anybody can deem “important”, and this value often decides whether a study is “important” or not. I think the authors really want to critique this approach, and suggest that denoting a study’s worth based on this value decreases our true understanding of the science behind it. The authors want to point out that turning away from this method will allow us to focus more on our understanding of the research and results. By distancing ourselves from this method we can think more critically about the theories behind it, the protocol and methods used for analysis, and the results that were found. To me, statistical thinking embodies this approach of critical thinking, and it also refers to understanding the theory behind tests or modeling techniques, knowing your data and how it was collection, and being able to really process what approaches would be beneficial to effectively communicate and analyze your data.

title: Advantages and Drawbacks of using P-values
section: Section 2, third paragraph: The authors state “A label of statistical significance adds nothing to what is already conveyed by the value of p ; in fact, this dichotomization of p-values makes matters worse.” Elaborate on what you think the authors means.
text:
Section 2, third paragraph: The authors state “A label of statistical significance adds nothing to what is already conveyed by the value of p ; in fact, this dichotomization of p-values makes matters worse.” Elaborate on what you think the authors means.
I think that this quote is portraying the idea that once you denote whether a p-value is significant or not, you have bestowed the idea that you should find the results important or not important. This quote is pointing out that declaring significance really means nothing, however the way it has been adapted into research has given it so much weight, and the true p-value number stands alone with or without a declaration of “significance”. The authors point out in this section that something people do not understand or often forget is the idea that the p-value just relates to the study, it is not a distinction that something is true or false. However that incorrect idea is often assumed due to the way we split p-values into two categories: significant and not significant. This harsh line between the two is harmful because again this value is made up, there is no real reason that 0.04 should be significant, but 0.058 shouldn’t be. To discourage this grouping approach, I think the authors want to really convey the idea that even without a label of significance the p-value still can display information to us about a study, and that due to the way we linguistically understand significance, we have transformed this classification (which is unnecessary!) into a very black and white approach to understanding scientific results.

title: Advantages and Drawbacks of using P-values
section: Section 2, end of first column: The authors state “For the integrity of scientific publishing and research dissemination, therefore, whether a p-value passes any arbitrary threshold should not be considered at all when deciding which results to present or highlight.” Do you agree or disagree? How should it be decided which results to present/highlight in scientific publishing?
text:
Section 2, end of first column: The authors state “For the integrity of scientific publishing and research dissemination, therefore, whether a p-value passes any arbitrary threshold should not be considered at all when deciding which results to present or highlight.” Do you agree or disagree? How should it be decided which results to present/highlight in scientific publishing?
I do agree with this statement, I think that publishing or focusing on only “significant” research would cause people to miss out on other studies which may have interesting conclusions, novel approaches, or new theories. By limiting the presentation of research we also limit the opportunities for studies to be replicated, and we miss out on understanding the full range of scientific possibilities. I will say that I do think that the p-value should be still communicated to your audience when applicable, but it shouldn’t be the basis of your results. I think that results should be presented or highlighted if they follow comprehensive protocols and show possible patterns which could be explained scientifically or align with theories/ideas that should be explored more. I think those presenting should be focused less on the threshold the p-value passes, and focus more on understanding the results and how they can affect or change current theories.

title: Advantages and Drawbacks of using P-values
section: Section 3, end of page 2: The authors state “The statistical community has not yet converged on a simple paradigm for the use of statistical inference in scientific research – and in fact it may never do so. A one-size-fits-all approach to statistical inference is an inappropriate expectation.” Do you agree or disagree? Explain.
text:
Section 3, end of page 2: The authors state “The statistical community has not yet converged on a simple paradigm for the use of statistical inference in scientific research – and in fact it may never do so. A one-size-fits-all approach to statistical inference is an inappropriate expectation.” Do you agree or disagree? Explain.
I agree with both of these statements, I think that due to the amount of scientific and humanitarian fields which utilize statistics it is unreasonable to think that there could be just one piece of criteria to judge all of these studies. The differences within fields should prompt us to use more than just one approach because different studies require different skill sets and it would be beneficial to approach different topics with different ideas in mind. I also think that even within a field there are still so many opinions, and people who may prioritize or argue for different criteria, that it would be unlikely you could agree on just one approach within a community. I also believe this is good, academia and research is a place where I think people should have the freedom to explore theories and to analyze results with different methods, as this will only expand our understanding of these studies. I think generally the norm for analyzing results should be with multiple ideas in mind because this increases not only your understanding, but the types of conclusions you can make. By idolizing one approach we can miss our on things the data may be able to convey to us.

title: Advantages and Drawbacks of using P-values
section: Section 3.2: The authors note that they are envisioning “a sort of ‘statistical thoughtfulness’.” What do you think “statistical thoughtfulness” means? What are some ways to demonstrate “statistical thoughtfulness” in an analysis?
text:
Section 3.2: The authors note that they are envisioning “a sort of ‘statistical thoughtfulness’.” What do you think “statistical thoughtfulness” means? What are some ways to demonstrate “statistical thoughtfulness” in an analysis?
Statistical thoughtfulness can refer to understanding the study, thinking critically about assumptions, and understanding your models/modeling approaches. This approach enables flexibility in your analysis, which is good as this can help more discoveries arise. Other important aspects to statistical thoughtfulness are asking questions about the study or the protocol to develop a theoretical understanding of your project, and by researching prior beliefs or studies. Lastly an important aspect is making your study reproducible, by doing so you are thinking ahead for those who may want to replicate your study and support/challenge your results. I think being statistically thoughtful includes thinking about the impact of your study, how will it impact what we already know, how will it impact those affected by this study, and how will it impact people who want to continue studying this topic. By including others in our thinking while we preform an analysis I think it increases your range of people you can affect, and it also then contributes more to the scientific field and topic. I think this idea is really important because accessibility and teamwork are really important ideas in the progression of research, and I think that they are things which can often be forgotten.

title: Advantages and Drawbacks of using P-values
section: Section 3.2.4: A few of the authors of papers in this special issue argue that some of the terminology used in statistics, such as “significance” and “confidence” can be misleading, and they propose the use of “compatibility” instead. What you do you think they believe the problem is? Do you agree or disagree (that there is a problem and that changing the name will help)?
text:
Section 3.2.4: A few of the authors of papers in this special issue argue that some of the terminology used in statistics, such as “significance” and “confidence” can be misleading, and they propose the use of “compatibility” instead. What you do you think they believe the problem is? Do you agree or disagree (that there is a problem and that changing the name will help)?
I think that the issue with these specific words is the way that we are known to understand them, and this can cause overconfidence in connection and causation. The words significance and confidence suggest the idea that things are connected, and that we know that connection to be true. This is misleading because in reality p-values or confidence intervals do not tell us any true fact, they are just calculations created from our data. By using the word “compatibility,” you suggest the idea that your data aligns with particular idea, but not that it must be true. Honestly, I have a bit of trouble fully agreeing with this argument, I think that there is a problem and that a lot of people probably do take p-values and confidence intervals at face value, believing them to be fact or that they prove something to be true. However, I think that believing that just changing the words to something will likely not solve the problem, and the problem is in the weight and importance we have given to the criteria. I think although it is true these words suggest different things, the main problem lies in the fact that we have limited a lot of research to just the numerical outputs of p-values and confidence intervals. By changing that approach and expanding the amount of criteria we consider and by looking closer at the results themselves, I think we would distribute the weights these values have, and then this issue of terminology may not be so prevalent.

section: Find a quote or point that really strikes you (i.e., made you think). What is the quote (and tell me where to find it), and why does it stand out to you?
text:
Find a quote or point that really strikes you (i.e., made you think). What is the quote (and tell me where to find it), and why does it stand out to you?
The quote that I chose is, “Indeed, there is essentially no aspect of scientific investigation in which judgement is not required,” which appears under section 3.3.1 in the second paragraph. I chose this quote because I think it conveys a really important idea about the way that science connects people. I think it can be common that as you research something and dedicate time to it, you don’t really want to hear about somebody’s judgement or opinion about your choices. However, this quote makes me think about how without that judgement there is no way for you to get better, and the judgement of someone else is what leads to not just the advancement of your ideas, but it keeps the research topic alive. On that topic, this quote also makes me think about the idea that the research everybody carries out is initially due to some type of judgement, whether of another study or a concept. Judgement has likely been a driving force in a majority of our scientific advancements, and this is an idea I really have never thought about. Lastly, I think the word judgement carries a lot of negative connotations, but I like the way that it was used in this quote because it shows how judgement can actually be a really positive and impactful thing.
